title: Inside the Rosette Nebula
caption: Part of the Rosette Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Rosette Nebula · constellation Monoceros · about 5,200 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Released for Hubble’s 35th anniversary, April 2025 (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Dark clouds of hydrogen gas mixed with dust stand in silhouette across this Hubble close-up of the Rosette Nebula. The Rosette is a large star-forming region about 100 light-years across, some 5,200 light-years away. Hubble’s view covers just a small piece of it, about 4 light-years wide, roughly the distance from the Sun to its neighbor Alpha Centauri.
The dark clouds are being worn away and shaped by fierce radiation from the cluster of big stars at the center of the nebula, outside this frame.

At the upper right, a young star buried at the tip of a dark cloud is launching jets of plasma. Where they slam into the cold gas around it, they make a shock wave, which glows red. The other colors come from hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen in the nebula.
scale: This view is about 4 light-years across, according to the release. Its light set out about 5,200 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble’s cameras through six filters, including narrowband filters for oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen. The color assigned to each filter isn’t published. The caption says the colors come from hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the colors are assigned, so the eye would not see this palette.

behind.people: See full credit: NASA, ESA, STScI
behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: This picture was part of Hubble’s 35th-anniversary celebration in April 2025, which revisited favorite targets with new views.
alt: Dark, wispy clouds of dust silhouetted against glowing gas, with a small red glow at upper right where a jet strikes the surrounding gas.
